title: Bandeja Paisa
shortDescription: Colombia's iconic platter with beans, rice, chicharrón, chorizo, eggs, and avocado
note: Colombia's most famous dish from the Paisa region—a hearty feast on one plate.
introCopy: Bandeja Paisa is the crown jewel of Colombian cuisine, a generous platter that brings together red beans, white rice, ground beef, chicharrón, chorizo, fried eggs, plantain, avocado, and arepa. Originating in Antioquia, this dish was fuel for farmers and laborers, and today it's a celebration of abundance and tradition.

steps.text: Cook the beans: In a large pot, combine soaked beans, water, onion, garlic, cumin, and salt. Bring to a boil, then reduce heat and simmer for 60–75 minutes until beans are tender. Add water if needed.
Make chicharrón: In a heavy skillet, cook pork belly chunks over medium heat in their own fat until deeply golden and crispy, about 30 minutes. Drain on paper towels.
Cook chorizo: In the same skillet, fry chorizo links until browned and cooked through, about 10 minutes. Set aside.
Cook ground beef: Season ground beef with cumin and paprika. Cook in a skillet over medium-high heat until browned and crumbled, about 8 minutes.
Fry plantains: Heat oil in a skillet and fry plantain slices until golden on both sides, about 3 minutes per side. Drain on paper towels.
Fry eggs: Fry eggs sunny-side up or over-easy to your preference.
Assemble each bandeja paisa: On a large plate, arrange rice, beans, ground beef, chicharrón, chorizo, fried egg, fried plantain, avocado slices, and an arepa. Serve immediately.

title: Ajiaco Santafereño
shortDescription: Bogotá's iconic chicken and potato soup with guascas and corn
note: A soul-warming soup that defines Bogotá's culinary identity.
introCopy: Ajiaco is Bogotá's most beloved dish—a thick, creamy chicken soup with three types of potatoes, corn, and the distinctive herb guascas. Served with capers, cream, avocado, and rice, it's comfort in a bowl and a tribute to the Andean highlands.

steps.text: In a large pot, combine chicken, water, onion, garlic, and scallions. Bring to a boil, then reduce heat and simmer for 30 minutes until chicken is cooked through.
Remove chicken from pot. Once cool enough to handle, shred the meat and discard bones and skin. Set aside.
Strain the broth and return it to the pot. Add all three types of potatoes and corn. Simmer for 25 minutes.
The russet potatoes will begin to dissolve and thicken the soup. Add guascas, salt, and pepper. Simmer for another 10 minutes.
Return shredded chicken to the pot and heat through, about 5 minutes.
Serve hot in deep bowls with heavy cream, capers, avocado slices, and white rice on the side for guests to add as desired.

title: Arepas con Queso
shortDescription: Colombian cheese-stuffed corn cakes, crispy outside and melty inside
note: The quintessential Colombian breakfast and anytime snack.
introCopy: Arepas are to Colombia what bread is to France—a daily staple and a source of regional pride. These golden corn cakes are stuffed with salty, melty cheese and griddled until crispy. Serve them for breakfast with hot chocolate, or alongside any meal.

steps.text: In a large bowl, mix masarepa and salt. Gradually add warm water, mixing with your hands until a smooth, pliable dough forms. It should be moist but not sticky. Let rest for 5 minutes.

Divide dough into 8 equal portions. Flatten each into a disc, place a piece of cheese in the center, and fold dough around it, sealing completely. Gently flatten into a round patty about 1/2 inch thick.
Heat a griddle or large skillet over medium heat. Add butter. Cook arepas for 5–6 minutes per side until golden brown and crispy on the outside.
Serve immediately while cheese is melted and gooey.

title: Empanadas Colombianas
shortDescription: Crispy corn turnovers filled with spiced beef and potatoes
note: Street food favorite—golden, crunchy, and packed with flavor.
introCopy: Colombian empanadas are made with a corn-based dough and deep-fried to crispy perfection. The filling is a savory mix of ground beef, potatoes, and hogao (Colombian tomato-onion sauce), with a hint of cumin and sazón. Serve with ají and lime for the full experience.

steps.text: Make the filling: Heat 2 tbsp oil in a skillet. Sauté onion, tomatoes, and garlic until softened, about 5 minutes. Add ground beef and cook until browned, breaking up with a spoon.
Add diced potatoes, cumin, paprika, salt, and pepper. Add 1/2 cup water, cover, and simmer until potatoes are tender, about 12 minutes. Let cool completely.
Make the dough: In a bowl, mix masarepa and salt. Gradually add warm water, kneading until smooth and pliable. Cover with a damp towel.
Divide dough into 12 balls. Place each between two sheets of plastic wrap and flatten into a 5-inch circle. Place 2 tbsp filling on one half, fold over, and press edges to seal firmly.
Heat oil in a deep pot to 350°F (175°C). Fry empanadas in batches until golden and crispy, about 4–5 minutes per batch. Drain on paper towels.
Serve hot with ají sauce and lime wedges.

title: Sancocho Trifásico
shortDescription: Hearty Colombian soup with three meats, plantains, yuca, and corn
note: A celebratory stew that brings family and friends together.
introCopy: Sancocho is the heart of Colombian gatherings—a robust, soul-satisfying soup made with three meats (chicken, beef, and pork), root vegetables, plantains, and corn. Every region has its own version, but sancocho trifásico from the Valle del Cauca is one of the most beloved.

steps.text: In a large pot, combine beef ribs, pork ribs, chicken, water, scallions, onion, and garlic. Bring to a boil, skimming any foam. Reduce heat and simmer for 45 minutes.
Add yuca, plantains, corn, and potatoes. Season with cumin, salt, and pepper. Simmer for another 35–40 minutes until all vegetables are tender.
Stir in fresh cilantro. Taste and adjust seasoning.
Serve hot in large bowls with white rice, avocado slices, and ají sauce on the side.

title: Lechona Tolimense
shortDescription: Festive roasted pork stuffed with rice, peas, and spices
note: Colombia's ultimate celebration roast—crispy skin and savory filling.
introCopy: Lechona is a spectacular whole roasted pig stuffed with seasoned rice, peas, and pork, traditional to the Tolima region. It's the centerpiece of festivals and family celebrations, with crackling golden skin and a rich, spiced filling. Served with arepas and ají, it's pure Colombian joy.

steps.text: Make the filling: In a large pan, cook diced pork shoulder until browned and tender, about 20 minutes. Add onion and garlic, sauté until soft.
Stir in cooked rice, peas, cumin, paprika, achiote, salt, and pepper. Mix well and cook for 5 minutes. Let cool completely.
Prepare the pork belly: Score the skin in a crosshatch pattern. Rub the inside (meat side) with salt and oil.
Spread the rice filling evenly over the inside of the pork belly. Roll tightly and tie securely with kitchen twine at 2-inch intervals.
Preheat oven to 325°F (160°C). Place lechona seam-side down in a roasting pan. Roast for 4–5 hours until skin is crispy and internal temperature reaches 165°F.
Let rest for 15 minutes, then slice and serve with arepas and ají sauce.

title: Patacones
shortDescription: Crispy twice-fried green plantains—Colombia's favorite side
note: Crunchy, salty, and irresistible—the perfect accompaniment.
introCopy: Patacones (also called tostones) are twice-fried green plantain slices that are crispy on the outside and tender inside. They're served alongside almost everything in Colombia—from soups to seafood to grilled meats. Top with salt, ají, or hogao for extra flavor.

steps.text: Cut each plantain diagonally into 1.5-inch thick slices.
Heat oil in a deep skillet to 350°F (175°C). Fry plantain slices in batches for 3–4 minutes until lightly golden but not fully cooked. Remove and drain on paper towels.
Place each fried slice between two sheets of parchment paper and flatten with a flat-bottomed plate or tostonera to about 1/4 inch thick.
Return flattened plantains to hot oil and fry again for 2–3 minutes per side until golden and crispy.
Drain on paper towels and sprinkle with salt while hot. Serve immediately.

title: Arroz con Coco
shortDescription: Sweetened coconut rice from Colombia's Caribbean coast
note: Fragrant, subtly sweet, and utterly addictive.
introCopy: This coastal specialty is made by toasting grated coconut until golden, then simmering rice in coconut milk with sugar and a hint of cinnamon. The result is fluffy, slightly sweet rice with a gorgeous golden color and rich coconut flavor—perfect alongside fried fish or seafood stews.

steps.text: In a large pot over medium heat, toast grated coconut, stirring constantly, until golden brown, about 8–10 minutes.
Add water and coconut milk to the pot. Bring to a boil, then strain out the toasted coconut solids (optional, or leave in for texture). Return liquid to pot.
Add rice, brown sugar, salt, cinnamon, and raisins (if using). Stir well and bring to a boil.
Reduce heat to low, cover, and simmer for 20 minutes until rice is tender and liquid is absorbed.
Remove from heat and let rest, covered, for 5 minutes. Fluff with a fork and serve.

title: Changua
shortDescription: Bogotá's traditional milk and egg soup with scallions and cilantro
note: A humble, comforting breakfast soup unique to the highlands.
introCopy: Changua is Bogotá's most distinctive breakfast—a simple soup of milk, water, scallions, and poached eggs, finished with fresh cilantro. It's warming, nourishing, and utterly comforting on chilly Andean mornings. Serve with calado (toasted bread) and a sprinkle of cheese.

steps.text: In a medium pot, combine milk, water, scallions, and salt. Bring to a gentle simmer over medium heat.
Carefully crack eggs one at a time into the simmering liquid. Poach for 3–4 minutes until whites are set but yolks are still runny.
Remove from heat and stir in fresh cilantro.
Ladle soup and one egg into each bowl. Serve with toasted bread and crumbled queso fresco on top.

title: Buñuelos Colombianos
shortDescription: Crispy fried cheese fritters—a Christmas tradition
note: Golden, airy, and cheesy—Colombia's most beloved holiday treat.
introCopy: Buñuelos are Colombia's iconic Christmas fritters, made with fresh cheese, cornstarch, and yuca starch, then deep-fried until golden and puffy. They're crispy outside, light and airy inside, with a subtle cheese tang. Enjoyed year-round, but essential during the holidays alongside natilla and hot chocolate.

steps.text: In a large bowl, combine crumbled cheese, cornstarch, tapioca starch, baking powder, salt, and sugar. Mix well.
Add eggs and knead until a smooth, pliable dough forms. It should be slightly sticky but hold its shape.
Roll dough into 20 small balls, about 1.5 inches in diameter. Keep hands lightly oiled to prevent sticking.
Heat oil in a deep pot to 325°F (160°C). Fry buñuelos in batches, turning frequently, until golden brown and puffed, about 5–6 minutes per batch.
Drain on paper towels. Serve warm or at room temperature.

title: Sobrebarriga al Horno
shortDescription: Colombian baked beef flank in tomato-beer sauce with panela
note: Tender, flavorful, and deeply satisfying—a Sunday classic.
introCopy: Sobrebarriga is flank steak braised until melt-in-your-mouth tender, then baked in a rich tomato sauce sweetened with panela (unrefined cane sugar) and beer. It's a beloved Sunday lunch dish, traditionally served with rice, potatoes, and salad.

steps.text: In a large pot, combine flank steak, water, quartered onion, smashed garlic, and salt. Bring to a boil, then reduce heat and simmer for 90 minutes until beef is very tender.
Remove beef and let cool slightly. Strain and reserve 1 cup of the cooking liquid. Slice beef against the grain into thin strips.
Preheat oven to 350°F (175°C). In a large skillet, heat oil and sauté diced onion, tomatoes, and garlic until softened, about 8 minutes.
Add beer, reserved cooking liquid, panela, cumin, and black pepper. Simmer for 10 minutes until sauce thickens slightly.
Arrange sliced beef in a baking dish. Pour sauce over the top. Cover with foil and bake for 30 minutes.
Serve hot with white rice and boiled potatoes.

title: Pandebono
shortDescription: Colombian cheese bread rolls with yuca starch—warm, chewy, addictive
note: Gluten-free, cheesy, and perfect with coffee.
introCopy: Pandebono is a beloved Colombian breakfast bread from the Valle del Cauca region. Made with yuca starch, cornmeal, and fresh cheese, these rolls are naturally gluten-free, with a chewy texture and salty-sweet flavor. Best enjoyed warm from the oven with hot chocolate or coffee.

steps.text: Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Line a baking sheet with parchment paper.
In a large bowl, combine tapioca starch, masarepa, grated cheese, and salt. Mix well.
Add eggs and melted butter. Knead with your hands until a smooth, pliable dough forms. If too dry, add milk 1 tablespoon at a time.
Divide dough into 12 portions and roll each into a ball. Place on the prepared baking sheet, spaced apart.
Bake for 18–20 minutes until golden and puffed.
Serve warm. Store leftovers and reheat in the oven for best texture.

title: Cazuela de Mariscos
shortDescription: Caribbean seafood stew with coconut milk, shrimp, fish, and squid
note: Rich, creamy, and brimming with ocean flavor.
introCopy: Cazuela de Mariscos is Colombia's coastal treasure—a luscious seafood stew made with coconut milk, tomatoes, peppers, and a bounty of fresh seafood. Originating from Cartagena and the Caribbean coast, it's vibrant, aromatic, and deeply satisfying. Serve with arroz con coco and patacones.

steps.text: Heat oil in a large pot or cazuela over medium heat. Sauté onion, bell pepper, and garlic until softened, about 5 minutes.
Add diced tomatoes, cumin, paprika, salt, and pepper. Cook for 5 minutes until tomatoes break down.
Pour in coconut milk and seafood stock. Bring to a simmer and cook for 10 minutes.
Add fish chunks and simmer for 5 minutes until fish is nearly cooked through.
Add shrimp, squid, and clams/mussels. Simmer for another 5–7 minutes until shrimp are pink and shellfish have opened. Discard any unopened shells.
Stir in fresh cilantro. Serve hot with arroz con coco.

title: Tamales Colombianos
shortDescription: Corn dough parcels filled with pork, chicken, vegetables, and eggs
note: A labor of love wrapped in banana leaves—worth every minute.
introCopy: Colombian tamales are a celebration wrapped in banana leaves. Corn masa is filled with seasoned pork, chicken, potatoes, carrots, peas, and hard-boiled eggs, then steamed to tender perfection. Regional variations abound, but all share the same spirit of abundance and tradition. Serve with hot chocolate.

steps.text: Make the masa: In a large bowl, combine masa harina, oil, warm stock, cumin, paprika, and salt. Mix until smooth and spreadable. Set aside.

Prepare the filling: In a pot, cook pork and chicken in salted water until tender, about 25 minutes. Drain and set aside. In the same pot, cook potatoes, carrot, and peas until tender, about 10 minutes. Drain.

Assemble tamales: Lay two banana leaves in a cross pattern. Spread 1/2 cup masa in the center. Top with a portion of pork, chicken, vegetables, peas, and half a hard-boiled egg. Season with salt and pepper.
Fold banana leaves over filling to form a rectangular packet. Tie securely with twine. Repeat for all 12 tamales.
Steam tamales: Stand tamales upright in a large steamer pot with 2 inches of water. Cover and steam for 2 hours, adding water as needed.
Let rest for 10 minutes before unwrapping. Serve hot with hot chocolate.

title: Mondongo Colombiano
shortDescription: Traditional tripe soup with vegetables, chorizo, and spices
note: A hearty, restorative soup treasured across Colombia.
introCopy: Mondongo is a beloved Colombian tripe soup, rich with vegetables, pork, and spices. It's a weekend tradition, often enjoyed as a remedy after a night out. The tripe becomes tender and flavorful after long simmering, and the soup is served with rice, avocado, and arepas for a complete meal.

ingredients.prepNote: cleaned and cut into small pieces

steps.text: In a large pot, combine tripe, pork ribs, water, scallions, onion, and garlic. Bring to a boil, skimming foam. Reduce heat and simmer for 90 minutes until tripe is tender.
Add yuca, potatoes, carrot, plantain, cumin, paprika, salt, and pepper. Simmer for another 40–45 minutes until vegetables are tender.
Stir in fresh cilantro. Taste and adjust seasoning.
Serve hot in deep bowls with white rice, avocado slices, and arepas on the side.
